name: Anterior pelvic tilt correction

lead: Anterior pelvic tilt correction bundles hip flexor stretches with glute and core exercises to reduce forward pelvic tilt and the lower-back arch. Proponents cite a flatter-looking stomach, better posture and, in some accounts, more apparent height.

The idea is that shortened hip flexors and weak glutes and abdominals pull the pelvis forward, so lengthening the former and strengthening the latter rebalances it. Encyclopedic sources describe the same approach but flag weak referencing, and no controlled study tests it for appearance.

paras: The usual package is hip flexor stretching, glute bridges, and core work such as planks, side planks and dead bugs, done a few times a week and combined with less sitting. Posture changes are described as building over weeks.
Exercise itself is low risk, but hyperlordosis can accompany back pain, disc problems or structural conditions that a clinician would assess. Persistent back pain warrants clinical assessment.

chain: Stretch hips, strengthen glutes and core
angle.text: Proponents use this routine to reduce pelvic tilt, citing a flatter-looking stomach, better posture and in some accounts more apparent height. Stretching tight hip flexors and strengthening glutes and core is meant to bring the pelvis back toward neutral.

lead: Anterior pelvic tilt (APT) is described as a posture in which the front of the pelvis drops relative to the back, often accompanied by an exaggerated lower-back arch known as lumbar hyperlordosis. [1] In looksmaxxing and fitness communities, APT correction refers to a package of stretches and strengthening exercises intended to reduce that tilt, with proponents citing a flatter-looking stomach, better posture and, in some accounts, increased apparent height. [1]

The usual package is hip flexor stretching, glute strengthening and core work such as glute bridges, planks, side planks and dead bugs. [1] Wikipedia notes that this recommendation relies on a consumer-health source and that the article needs better references. [1]

Medical sources describe lumbar hyperlordosis as associated with prolonged sitting, weak abdominal and gluteal muscles, tight hip flexors and hamstrings, excess visceral fat and pregnancy, as well as structural conditions. [2] No controlled trial found tests an APT correction program for appearance.
infobox: Hip flexor stretch, glute and core strengthening

paras: Wikipedia describes APT as one of several pelvic tilt patterns, and links the term to lumbar hyperlordosis. [1] Lateral tilt, by contrast, is associated with scoliosis and leg-length differences. [1] Hyperlordosis is typically assessed by lateral X-ray; one cited normal range is 20 to 60 degrees, though other studies report values up to roughly 85 degrees, and the curve is generally larger in females. [2]

Corrective exercise described in medical encyclopedias consists of stretching the hip flexors and lower back and strengthening the abdominals, glutes and hamstrings, sometimes over several months and alongside less sitting. [2] Other measures mentioned include bracing for certain disc problems and manipulative therapy, whose effectiveness the same article calls controversial. [2]

Posture and gym communities add related drills such as the couch stretch, glute bridges, plank variations, the McGill Big 3 and scapular work for upper-back posture, which are covered in their own articles.

The Wikipedia articles on pelvic tilt and lordosis carry maintenance tags for needing more reliable medical references, and the exercise recommendations rest on limited sources. [1][2] The pelvic tilt article's academic citation concerns how spinopelvic terms are defined, not treatment outcomes. [1] The lordosis article advises that people with back pain or suspected lordosis consult a clinician for diagnosis. [2]

Associated conditions listed for hyperlordosis include lower back pain, possible disc damage and, in some medical conditions, structural causes such as spondylolisthesis, osteoporosis or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which are not addressed by self-directed exercise. [2]

No studies found testing an anterior pelvic tilt correction routine for appearance. The pelvic tilt article cites a 2024 study of posterior tilt in chronic low back pain, which is a different condition. [1]
